analysis.one_liner: Restores taxes on oil and chemical companies to fund toxic waste site cleanups through 2017.
analysis.headline: Introduced by nine Democratic senators in September 2008, the bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a vote before the Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would bring back two taxes that used to pay for the Superfund, the federal program that cleans up the nation's worst toxic waste sites. One is an excise tax on petroleum and hazardous chemicals; the other is a tax on corporations. Both expired in the mid-1990s, and since then cleanup costs have been paid out of general tax revenue — meaning ordinary taxpayers, not the polluting companies, cover the bill. This bill would put that cost back on oil, chemical, and other companies through the end of 2017.
analysis.who_benefits: People living near Superfund toxic waste sites benefit most: cleanup money would come from a dedicated tax on polluting companies rather than from general tax revenue. Taxpayers broadly benefit because the cost of cleaning up hazardous waste shifts back to the companies whose products create it.

how_it_helps.text: The bill reinstates the Hazardous Substance Superfund financing rate — an excise tax on petroleum and hazardous substances — applying it again from enactment through January 1, 2017.
It also reinstates the corporate environmental income tax, a separate tax on corporations, for taxable years through 2017.

Together these taxes refill the Superfund trust fund, which pays for cleaning up abandoned hazardous waste sites, shifting the cost from general taxpayers to the companies whose products created the waste.

analysis.who_pays: Oil companies, chemical manufacturers, and other corporations pay through the reinstated excise and corporate taxes. Some of the petroleum excise tax could be passed along to consumers in fuel prices.

drawbacks.text: The bill reinstates an excise tax on crude oil and petroleum products, and taxes like this are typically passed through to consumers in prices at the pump, so part of the cost could land on ordinary people.
The reinstated taxes only run until January 1, 2017, so the funding fix is temporary and would need to be renewed again.
Restoring the taxes refills the fund but does not itself speed up the pace of cleaning up toxic sites, which depends on the Environmental Protection Agency's cleanup program.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit is real: it would shift cleanup costs from general taxpayers back to the companies whose substances create hazardous waste sites, putting the Superfund trust fund on dedicated footing through 2017. The main costs are that excise taxes on petroleum tend to show up in fuel prices, so part of the burden could land on consumers, and that a dedicated tax does not by itself speed up the slow pace of site cleanups. On balance, the bill's design is straightforward and its main effect is a transfer of cleanup costs from ordinary taxpayers to polluting industries.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee in September 2008 and sat there with no further action until the Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on September 23, 2008, read twice, and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance.
The action history shows no further steps — no committee vote, no floor action — before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.
The bill had nine Democratic Senate sponsors: Clinton, Boxer, Lautenberg, Cardin, Obama, Biden, Nelson of Florida, Wyden, and Dodd.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil, chemical, and other corporations that would have paid the reinstated taxes came out ahead: they continue to pay nothing into the Superfund, and general taxpayers keep covering hazardous waste cleanups through ordinary revenue.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and chemical companies; taxpayers keep paying

industries.note: The bill reinstates the Hazardous Substance Superfund financing rate, an excise tax on crude oil and petroleum products, through the end of 2017. This tax has not applied since it lapsed at the end of 1995, and since then Superfund cleanups have been paid from general taxpayer revenue rather than by the industry.

Hazardous substances are subject to the reinstated Superfund excise tax, and the corporate environmental income tax also applies to chemical companies. The industry's interest in keeping the tax lapsed runs against communities left with toxic waste cleanup bills.
The corporate environmental income tax is a broad corporate tax, so reinstating it raises the tax bill of profitable corporations generally, not just polluters, through 2017.
With the polluter taxes lapsed, ordinary taxpayers have been footing Superfund cleanup costs through general revenue; the bill shifts that burden back to the companies that generate hazardous waste.
